July 31, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Leonid Andronov Record low water levels in Europe's major rivers have curtailed the transport of goods, reduced electricity output and shrunk company earnings, stoking fears about the economic impact of searing heat and erratic rainfall. As Europe experiences the fastest warming of any continent and record-breaking heatwaves, drought has exposed the need to reconsider business practices. From the bustling port of Rotterdam to hydropower plants in Serbia, waterways have become a less reliable way to transport goods such as grains and oil, or to produce much-needed electricity when millions are seeking to cool their homes. "It's affecting not one region like we've seen in the past, but the whole European landscape," said Alessandro Armenia, a power analyst at commodities data and analytics firm Kpler. "Given the current dynamics, it means either we're going to see blackouts or we need to invest way more." HYDROPOWER AND NUCLEAR OUTPUT CUT Production of nuclear power in Hungary and hydropower in Serbia have fallen because of record low water levels along the Danube, which passes through major cities like Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade on its route from Germany to the Black Sea. The Paks nuclear power plant, which generates nearly half of Hungary's electricity, will be shut down on Monday, possibly for weeks because water levels on the river, which supplies cooling water to the facility, are expected to stay too low for it to operate safely. At Djerdap 1, Serbia's largest hydropower plant, output has fallen to 20% of capacity, the plant's production director Davor Maljokovic told Reuters, as the once broad shipping channel beside it has shrunk to expose sandbanks and gravel bars. The lack of water has also disrupted cooling systems at Serbia's Kostolac coal-fired power plants, forcing them to cut output, Serbia's state EPS power utility said. Both Serbia and Hungary say they will make up for the losses by importing electricity, a costly measure when demand on the spot market is high. Romania's state nuclear power producer Nuclearelectrica also had to shut one of its two reactors earlier this week for the same reason, with the second expected to soon follow, potentially depriving the country of a fifth of its electricity needs. France has also had to reduce nuclear power generation because of low water levels or rising river temperatures. WATER LEVELS ALSO DISRUPT TRANSPORT Energy is not the only loser. Cezar Gheorghe of Romanian grain market consultancy AGRIColumn told Reuters on Friday farmers along the Danube were having problems shipping their crops because low water levels stopped barges from using several river ports. “Only the ports which are closer to the Black Sea are still operational. Barges can’t go through the others,” Gheorghe said. “Crops buyers could offer farmers lower prices and load them in trucks, although there might also be a shortage of trucks.” Meanwhile, the volume of cargo transported to and from Rotterdam - Europe's largest sea port - to the Rhine has fallen slightly each week since the beginning of July and is around 10% lower than normal, a port spokesperson told Reuters. Chemical and oil product tankers and dry bulk carriers are particularly affected because of their normally greater draught compared to container barges, which means they sit deeper in the water and require greater water depths. DROUGHT REDUCES COMPANY EARNINGS Apart from the natural devastation of wildfires and temperatures that have caused thousands of excess deaths, companies' balance sheets have suffered from the changing climate. Austrian utility Verbund, which produced about 85% of its electricity from hydropower last year, said on Thursday that drought conditions reduced earnings by about €370 million in the first half compared with a year of normal hydrological conditions. French state-owned utility EDF said on Friday that full-year earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for 2026 were expected to fall by 10% because of low market prices and as heatwaves reduced power output. In Italy, the Po River basin has entered a state of high water scarcity, threatening rice crops and drinking water supplies across the north. Chief Executive of regional utility A2A, Renato Mazzoncini, said he expected hydropower production this year of 3.9 TWh compared to a historical average of 4.1. "Some of our reservoirs are under pressure," he said. "We practically need to start doing a rain dance." By SAM McNEIL ELSENBORN, Belgium (AP) — The wildfires burning across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames. Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg province in 1944. Fueled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent’s “climatic luck” is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies. Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant. “Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable,” Njeri said. Fires can ignite old munitions but can also burn away the scrub and brush that hides them. This wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived. Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, according to a study issued last month by the World Weather Attribution group. Flames chewed up old battlefields and set off buried explosives As they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns fell silent. In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be World War II-era ammunition. In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Gov. Hervé Jamar said “a few sporadic detonations” were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area. He said no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb. During World War II, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province’s dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens. In the first four years after Germany’s surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said Bernard Collard, a local historian who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium’s border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war. “When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are,” he said. He remembers his father detonating a found bomb in a quarry. The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smoldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around the High Fens. The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 American and 28,000 German troops. Every year, Belgium responds to thousands of calls about explosives Collard is authorized to scan with a metal detector the former battlefields, now forests, pastures and farmland. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases, and once, a human skeleton. “You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn’t take it lightly,” Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site. Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire. He frequently works with the Belgian demining squad. “It’s part of our history. We live with it,” Collard said. Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires because heat can trigger the explosives, said Jonas Tepe, a spokesperson for North Rhine-Westphalia, just across the border in Germany. The Belgian Ministry of Defense said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a “hot spot” compared to elsewhere in Belgium. Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres — infamous for harrowing trench warfare in World War I — call the annual tilling of the soil “ the iron harvest ” because it turns up so many war remnants. Every year across the nation, Belgium’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tons of munitions left over from both world wars. Flames are not the only threat Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons. In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest’s Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from World War II emerged at its base in receding water. As the Rhine dried up, German authorities also found a WWII-era bomb . Christina Greene, a researcher at the University of Arizona who, with Njeri, wrote an article on Europe’s wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said “the legacy of war keeps creeping up” because of climate change. “It’s reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven’t had to deal with in a while in certain places.” ___ Associated Press writers Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands; Sylvain Plazy in Brussels; Angela Charlton in Paris; Kirsten Grieshaber in Berlin; and Stanislav Hodina in Prague contributed to this report. https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/07/afd-germ.text: Elections in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend saw a decisive victory for the far-right AfD. While the eastern state is one of the smallest in the country, the result is being viewed as hugely significant and is set to pile pressure on the unpopular government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Upcoming pro-growth reforms and Germany's planned increase in defense and infrastructure spending are unlikely to be derailed, according to bank Berenberg, but further gains for the AfD will raise questions over national policymaking. A landslide electoral victory for the far-right in the small but significant state of Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend is sending shockwaves through Europe and piling pressure on Germany's federal government. Alternative for Germany (AfD) secured the highest share of the vote at 43.8%, well above the 17.2% of the incumbent Christian Democratic Union Party (CDU), which also leads the country's national coalition under Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Initial results show the AfD securing 39 of 83 parliamentary seats, leaving it three seats short of an outright majority and uncertain over its ability to form a new state government. A so-called "firewall" sees other parties in Germany agree not to cooperate with far-right in a way that would give it political power. However, AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund said Monday that the party would hold discussions with "individual parliamentary groups or individual MPs" to see if they would support it in governing. In a press conference, Merz said the election showed the need for reform but said Germany's "institutions were resilient and stable." "This message is also directed at our friends in Europe and across the globe," he said, according to a Reuters report. The "extraordinary" result may be the "most consequential German state-election result of the postwar era," Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at consultancy Eurasia Group, said Monday. While the AfD has been growing in popularity for years , particularly in eastern Germany , the result raises the prospect of the hard right taking power in a German state for the first time since the Nazi era. At the state level, the party has pledged stringently anti-refugee and anti-migrant policies, including accelerating deportations and separating the children of refugees into different classrooms, while encouraging SMEs to use AI rather than migrant workers and financially incentivizing families to have more children. Voters "seeking a genuinely radical break" voted AfD, while liberal and left-wing voters swung to the Greens and Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD), squeezing the CDU from both sides, Rahman said in a note. If it continues, that trend could see upcoming elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin turn "a regional earthquake into a rolling national crisis," he added. Public 'furious' over state of German economy Saxony-Anhalt, a traditional hub for German chemicals and motor supplies, has "suffered disproportionately" from the post-unification collapse of east German industry and the recent spike in energy prices, Berenberg Chief Economist Holger Schmieding said in a Monday note. The result also deals a hammer blow to the federal government of Merz, who polling suggests is deeply unpopular . Questions over the future of German industry, innovation and welfare were dominant themes in the electoral race, Peter Altmaier, former Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy for the CDU, told CNBC on Monday. Though it was a state election, Altmaier said dissatisfaction with national-level answers to those questions contributed to the result. The public is "furious" and turning to challenger parties on both the left and right after five years of economic stagnation and a lack of job creation at a time when many traditional jobs are being lost in Germany, Altmaier continued. "We expected the worst, but this result yesterday night was a kind of disaster ... and of course it will affect political debates across the country and upcoming state elections in other states," Altmaier said. "Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest states, of course, and the German democracy is strong and resilient. But this is unprecedented, and it will be a matter of concern not only for us but also for our neighbors in Europe." On Monday, ministers in both Poland and France — also facing the prospect of mounting electoral gains for the far-right — called the German result worrying, according to local media reports. Spending reform The Saxony-Anhalt election alone is very unlikely to derail Germany's planned increases in defense and infrastructure spending or the majority of unpopular cuts and pro-growth reforms set to be passed this fall, Berenberg's Holger Schmieding said. Those include pension system savings , tax and health-care reforms and measures to reduce bureaucracy , as well as hikes to defense and infrastructure spending . "The alternative – namely to shy away from reforms to strengthen Germany's growth potential – would likely be even worse for the outlook for the coalition parties in the long run," he said. It also seems "more likely than not" that Merz and his coalition will "soldier on" until the end of their federal parliamentary term in early 2029, Schmieding said. However, that is largely due to a lack of alternatives — and the result is still a "huge blow" to the chancellor and adds to the risk of his government falling apart, Schmieding added. German markets were calm on Monday, with yields on government bonds, known as bunds, slightly higher, in line with the rest of Europe. George Lagarias, chief economist at Forvis Mazars, said the risk in Saxony and Germany as a whole was "a loss of centrist consensus which could hamstring decision-making and exacerbate present economic dislocations." "Rising debt to pay for defense, challenges to the export-driven economic model, geopolitical upheaval and limited government can eventually challenge Bunds' stature as the risk-free asset of Europe and Germany's ability to cheaply fund its growth," he told CNBC. "As it sits at the heart of the euro zone, worries over the German economy could reverberate across Europe. We are not there yet. But we shouldn't be completely comforted by the mild initial reaction as a proof of long-term stability either."

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: A high-ranking member of the Australian navy says it would be ‘very difficult’ to put a gender-diverse navy recruit into US training due to American policies prohibiting transgender service personnel. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP View image in fullscreen A high-ranking member of the Australian navy says it would be ‘very difficult’ to put a gender-diverse navy recruit into US training due to American policies prohibiting transgender service personnel. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP Australian military Gender-diverse Australian sailors barred from US submarines despite Aukus deal, documents reveal Defence briefing released under freedom of information laws shows ADF beholden to US directives when in training Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Doherty Sun 15 Nov 2026 09.00 EST Last modified on Sun 15 Nov 2026 14.13 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Aukus is effectively forcing the Australian navy to comply with a US ban on transgender people in the military with gender-diverse navy recruits prevented from starting a career in nuclear submarines because they would not be safe training on US boats. Internal Australian defence force documents show transgender and non-binary sailors and officers are explicitly banned from Australia’s nuclear submarine training program because of US policies. An internal defence briefing, released under freedom of information laws, said while ADF policy on equality and inclusion was unchanged, “ US government policy is different ”. Aukus deal is ‘living a lie’: Australia will never get nuclear submarines from US and both sides know it, Bob Carr says Read more “ADF personnel undertaking duty in the US (including training) are required to comply with US policy,” the briefing said. “Consequently, transgender and nonbinary ADF personnel and ADF career applicants are currently unable to commence the SSN [nuclear-powered attack submarines] training pathway.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Australia, without a nuclear submarine fleet of its own, has hundreds of sailors and officers training on US nuclear submarines and on US bases. At a women in defence event in October, Rear Adm Tish van Stralen was asked how the defence force was “managing the recruitment of gender-diverse and LGBTQ+ Australians into the nuclear submarine pathway” given the US directive. Van Stralen, one of the highest-ranking women in the Australian navy, said the ADF was a diverse and equal opportunity employer. But she said potential recruits for the nuclear submarine program were told the ADF was “subject to policies and laws in other countries, so we have to be very mindful”. “We also have an obligation, a duty of care to our people, so we do not want to put our people into any sort of harm’s way or anything that might adversely affect them. “I’m working very closely with navy at the moment and with the submarine agency around the training opportunities because it would be very difficult for me to put a gender-diverse person into that training at the moment.” Van Stralen said the navy would seek alternative career paths for gender-diverse recruits prohibited from the nuclear submarine program. She said the UK, Australia’s other Aukus partner, had “more liberal policies” and that training opportunities “may arise in the UK”. “We don’t want to disadvantage people because of it but we are subject to the laws and policies of the US when we are in their country.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion US moves came amid Aukus deal The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, last year issued a directive to his department “to eliminate all diversity , equity and inclusion offices and initiatives”. He also has sought to ban transgender personnel from joining the US military – repeatedly using offensive slurs in public statements – and ordered that transgender personnel be purged from the services. Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 – the first week of his second term as president – which banned transgender service personnel and said gender-diverse people were unfit to serve. Announcing military cuts in September amid continued attacks on diversity, Hegseth declared that the US military would accept “no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals”. Under the Aukus deal, it is proposed that Australia will buy three Virginia-class nuclear submarines from the US, beginning in 2032. In the lead-up to that, Australian sailors are training onboard US Virginia-class submarines and at US bases, while US-flagged nuclear submarines are porting in Australia. Crewing Australia’s proposed nuclear submarine fleet is likely to prove one of the Aukus agreement’s most critical, sustained challenges. Virginia-class submarines have a complement of 135, more than double the crew for Australia’s diesel-electric Collins-class submarines. Last week Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles , said the Aukus timeline presented the country with a significant “training challenge”. “ We just need to be training more people and that’s what we’re doing,” Marles said at HMAS Stirling, the West Australian port through which US nuclear-powered submarines have been rotating. The Australian defence department did not respond to questions from the Guardian about the impact of adhering to the US policy directive, including how many Australian service personnel have been prevented from undertaking nuclear submarine training. The government’s nuclear-powered submarine workforce strategy urges defence to “proactively expand the talent pool through active inclusion of underrepresented groups , including women, First Nations Australians, regional communities, and individuals who may not traditionally see themselves in technical or defence-related careers”. https://www.portfolio.hu/global/20261119.text: Hatalmas várakozások előzték meg a háromoldalú találkozót, mivel számos olyan téma merülhetett fel, ami globális hatásokkal járhat. Már előzetesen nagy médiafigyelem irányult az eseményre, szinte minden mozdulat külön elemzést kapott Sencsenben. Hszi Csin-ping kínai elnök viszonozta Donald Trumpnak az Amerikában kapott látványos diplomáciai gesztust: a repülőtéren ő fogadta az Egyesült Államok vezetőjét. Ez nem számít bevett szokásnak, közel hét évtizede ez volt az első alkalom, hogy a felemelkedő nagyhatalom legmagasabb rangú figurája megjelenik egy másik ország delegációjának fogadásán. Utoljára 1959-ben történt ilyen, akkor Mao Ce-tung várta a reptéren a szovjet vezetőt, Nyikita Hruscsovot. Hszi ezzel viszonozta a gesztust, korábban Trump üdvözölte már a kifutópályán a nagy riválist. A Népi Felszabadító Hadsereg (People’s Liberation Army – PLA) díszőrsége várakozott a repülőtéren, miközben vadászgépek húztak el az égen színes füstcsíkokat hagyva maguk után. WATCH: Chinese President Xi Jinping made a rare trip to the airport to greet U.S. President Donald Trump. https://t.co/n0JSJtrzbv Üdvözlöm Önöket ismét Kínában, és várom, hogy mélyreható eszmecserét folytathassunk Önökkel a kínai-amerikai kapcsolatokat, az ázsiai-csendes-óceáni együttműködést és a globális helyzetet érintő főbb kérdésekről, hogy előmozdítsuk Kína és az Egyesült Államok közötti konstruktív és stabil stratégiai kapcsolatot a tisztelet, a méltányosság és a kölcsönösség alapján Ezt a fogadtatást rögtön elkezdték a Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök érkezésénél tapasztaltakhoz hasonlítani. Őt Caj Csi várta a reptéren, aki a Kínai Kommunista Párt (KKP) egyik legfontosabb embere, sokan kifejezetten Hszi árnyékának tartják . Hiába a magas rangú fogadtatás, ez azért mégsem olyan, mintha maga az elnök ment volna az érkező repülőgép elé. A legnagyobb nemzetközi érdeklődést ezúttal nem a Kína és az Egyesült Államok közötti megbeszélések váltották ki, hanem a hetekkel ezelőtt beharangozott hármas tárgyalás Donald Trump, Hszi Csin-ping és Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök között. Az amerikai vezető várható programjáról előzetesen kiadott közlemény szerint ez az utolsó esemény, amin még részt vesz, ezt követően visszautazik az Egyesült Államokba. Sajtótájékoztató nem szerepelt a tervek között. Előzetesen komoly találgatást váltott ki, hogy a vezetők milyen témákat érinthetnek. Washington kifejezetten a nukleáris fegyverkezésről szeretett volna megbeszéléseket tartani, a világ három legnagyobb atomarzenáljával bíró hatalom vezetőjének találkozóján ez nagyon is aktuális téma. Úgy számoltak, hogy Trump a nukleáris ellenőrzésre vonatkozóan dobhat be ötleteket. Előzetesen, újságírói kérdésre ugyanakkor erről nem volt hajlandó beszélni. A másik téma, amit visszatérően emlegettek előzetesen, hogy szóba kerülhet, az a közel-keleti háború, ám ez egy kicsit ingoványosabb talaj. Amerika háborúban áll Iránnal, a legtöbb jel szerint az iszlamista rezsim kulcsfontosságú segítséget kap Moszkvától és Pekingtől. Ezek a fegyverek hozzájárulhattak több amerikaiak elleni találathoz is. A Fehér Ház vezetője erre vonatkozóan is kapott kérdéseket, ám azt tagadta, hogy a két másik hatalom segítségét kérné majd a konfliktus lezárásához. Hszi a vélekedések szerint sokkal inkább a kereskedelmi megállapodás, technológiai verseny rendezése felé terelte volna a beszélgetést, a látványos diplomáciai gesztusokból ítélve pedig kifejezetten úgy lehetett érzékelni, hogy Amerikával törekszik a megegyezésre. Putyin számára az orosz-ukrán háborúval kapcsolatos közös állásfoglalás kiadása jelentette volna a legnagyobb diplomáciai sikert, ugyanakkor már magával a találkozóval is sokat nyert, mivel a nemzetközi elszigeteltségének lebontását tudta ezzel sugározni. Felbukkant az orosz delegációnál egy aktatáska , ami a feltételezések szerint a nukleáris rakéták indítókódjait tartalmazza, ezzel határozottan jelezve, hogy Moszkva „miért kapott helyet” az megbeszéléseken.
